messages.author: 0e713d20fc7459b5
messages.subject: Citation fossil hooks?
parts:
Dear BioGeoBEARS group,

Is there a proper reference in the scientific literature on using hooks for fossil informed biogeographical analyses?

Thank you & Cheers,
Torsten

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Citation fossil hooks?
parts:
Hi Torsten -- I don't think there is a journal publication, but one of these might work:

Matzke, Nicholas J (2013). "Probabilistic Historical Biogeography: New Models for Founder-Event Speciation, Imperfect Detection, and Fossils Allow Improved Accuracy and Model-Testing." Ph.D. Thesis, U.C. Berkeley Department of Integrative BIology.
Proquest: http://search.proquest.com/docview/1526024556

Matzke, Nicholas J; Säilä, Laura (2017). Phylogenetic biogeography of fossil Canidae: combining models of imperfect detection, fossil databases as taphonomic controls, and Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping. Evolution 2017, Portland, Oregon. June 23-27, 2017. http://www.evolutionmeetings.org/evolution-2017---portland-oregon.html YouTube video at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Of6MTpYYzsM

...or the BioGeoBEARS package itself.

However, the "hooks" idea turns out to be basically same as the "sampled ancestor" concept in birth-death-serial-sampling trees with fossils, in that the postulated direct ancestor is represented as a side-branch in the newick tree structure, just with a branchlength of 0.0 (in BEAST2) or <0.00000001 (or whatever you set in BioGeoBEARS).

How these short/zero-length branches are interpreted for a particular model all depends on the programmer. In Lagrange, all branches are extended up to the present to make the tree ultrametric. In BioGeoBEARS, the original branchlengths are used, except for those very short "hooks", which the program interprets as direct ancestors, rather than cladogenesis events.

Cheers,
Nick
